title: Spring warmth had uncertain links to lilac flowering duration in four western US samples from 1956 to 2003
abstract: We tested whether warmer springs were linked to a shorter flowering display in common lilac. We used 10,288 paired first- and end-bloom records in four samples from the historic western US monitoring program. We split sites at 110 degrees west and years at 1981. Models had plant and year effects and a winter temperature control. All four spring slopes were negative, from -0.51 to -1.02 days per degree Celsius. All four intervals included zero after correction for four tests. Removing long gaps or flagged records, adding plant trends, and using adjacent-year changes kept the negative signs. These checks did not establish a common effect. Few state clusters, missing visit schedules, coarse monthly weather, and loss of sites in later years limit inference. The test measures seasonal weather associations. It does not estimate a causal climate-change effect, individual flower life, pollution effects, or pollinator response. The package contains selected source events, monthly temperature extracts, exact model samples, code, source hashes, and independent numerical checks.
